design_detail: Single-author narrative clinical review (Psychiatr Clin North Am 2013;36(2):261–275), written by an emergency physician and medical toxicologist at Indiana University. A footnote states that the article originally appeared in the August 2011 issue of Neurologic Clinics (volume 29, number 3), so the 2013 text is a reprint. Sections: history and epidemiology of methamphetamine manufacture and use; pharmacology and toxicology; neuropsychiatric complications (cognition, anxiety, depression, psychosis); formication (delusional parasitosis); punding (stereotypy); Parkinson's disease; choreoathetoid movements; dental caries ('meth mouth'); summary; a five-item Key Points box. No methods section: no search, eligibility criteria or appraisal. 113 references. No tables and no figures. The review is addressed in places to psychiatrists and in places to neurologists, reflecting its republication. Read as the NIH author manuscript in PMC.
can_establish: How a medical toxicologist summarized, in 2011 and again in 2013, the neurological and psychiatric features attributed to sustained methamphetamine use, and which primary sources each statement rests on, including the then-current arguments about Parkinson's disease.
cannot_establish: The frequency of any of these features in people who use methamphetamine, or that methamphetamine caused them, because the review reports a handful of second-hand percentages from small, old or differently-selected samples, with no intervals, no comparison groups and no appraisal, and several of the figures are traced here to sources that do not match the description given.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The cited clinical evidence is mostly old or small: 1960s–1970s case series of amphetamine and methylamphetamine psychosis from the United Kingdom, the United States and Sweden; Japanese studies of the post-war psychosis epidemic; Taiwanese studies of premorbid characteristics and relatives; one meta-analysis of neuropsychological studies; imaging and post-mortem studies of dopaminergic markers; a hospital-records study and a telephone survey on Parkinson's disease; and a dental literature of surveys and case series.
sample.selection_effects: Selection of sources is unstated and cannot be audited. The clinical phenomena described (psychosis, formication, punding, choreoathetoid movements, advanced dental disease) are drawn from people in treatment, hospital or forensic settings, so nothing in the review describes people who use methamphetamine outside those settings. Several key frequency figures come from single studies of other populations (people with HIV; people who used cocaine; amphetamine rather than methamphetamine).

exposure.measurement: Not described at review level for any cited study.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. The review states that psychosis is seen more readily with higher amounts used over prolonged periods, while the amounts, durations and times to onset reported in the literature are highly variable, as is the duration of psychotic symptoms (from about a week to indefinite). Route is mentioned only as snorting, smoking or injection crossing the blood-brain barrier rapidly. It reports methamphetamine's half-life as 12 hours against about 90 minutes for cocaine.
exposure.polysubstance: Barely addressed. Tobacco is discussed only as a possible protective factor for Parkinson's disease (87–92% of people who use methamphetamine smoke cigarettes versus 22% of the general population, cited to a review). Cocaine and MDMA are discussed as comparators, and the author states that the similarities between these stimulants make the discussion largely transferable to them.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable at review level; the review notes that reductions in dopamine transporters recovered significantly with abstinence longer than 12 months in one study.

comparison.controls: Not applicable at review level. Of the cited studies described with a comparison, one gave amphetamine to people with pre-existing chorea and to people without it, and one compared people with Parkinson's disease with their unaffected spouses.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review raises the point itself: it suggests that damaged episodic memory and executive function may precede drug use and predispose to it, that a predisposition may underlie punding, and that family history of mental illness predicts methamphetamine-associated psychosis. It cites no study with a pre-use measurement.

outcomes.instruments: Not specified at review level. Outcomes discussed: neuropsychological test performance (episodic memory, executive function, fine motor dexterity), anxiety, depression, psychosis and its symptom profile, formication, punding, parkinsonism, choreoathetoid movements, and dental caries and tooth wear.
outcomes.operationalization: Not defined for any outcome. 'Abnormalities on neuropsychiatric tests' is used without a cut-off; punding is defined descriptively as non-goal-directed repetitive activity; formication as the belief of being infested with and bitten by insects.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed; the review reports second-hand percentages without denominators, intervals or comparison groups, and one odds ratio. Figures given: about 40% of people who use methamphetamine have abnormalities on neuropsychiatric tests; about 40% of patients admitted to drug-treatment facilities report formication, rising to 70% among those who had ever had psychosis; punding in 26% (40 of 150) of people with amphetamine addiction interviewed by Rylander, and in 38% of 50 people addicted to cocaine, who spent on average 3 hours a day on such activities; cigarette smoking in 87–92% of people who use methamphetamine versus 22% of the general population; and an odds ratio of 8 (95% CI 1.6 to 41.4) for amphetamine exposure in people with Parkinson's disease compared with their unaffected spouses, with exposure about 27 years before symptom onset.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cannot be assessed for source selection. The review does present both sides of the Parkinson's question, and names the main competing explanations for the dopaminergic findings (different disorder; recovery with abstinence; compensatory down-regulation rather than damage; protection by smoking).

interpretation_gap.results_show: A clinical description of phenomena reported in people who use methamphetamine, with a small number of second-hand percentages from selected samples, and a balanced account of the Parkinson's debate in which the author states that the prevailing view is that methamphetamine use does not raise the risk, while two small studies suggest earlier onset or higher incidence and need confirmation.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The commentary and summary are causal and categorical in a way the cited evidence is not: methamphetamine is said to damage dopaminergic neurotransmission and to preferentially cause psychiatric complications, chronic use to have "devastating effects" on the central nervous system, and people who use methamphetamine to have deficits in memory and executive function, with no comparison figures and no acknowledgment that the cross-sectional studies behind these statements cannot separate pre-existing differences from drug effects (a possibility the body itself raises twice). The Key Points state that dopamine receptor antagonists are the most effective treatments for the chronic psychiatric manifestations, which no trial in the review supports: the body cites one 1974 study of a neuroleptic against amphetamine-induced symptoms and a 1992 hypothesis paper on formication. The statement that about 40% of people who use methamphetamine have abnormalities on neuropsychiatric tests is traced here to a study of people with HIV. Where the review is at its best is the Parkinson's section, where the hypotheses are set against each other and the weakness of the positive studies is named.

timeline.event: Ellinwood's description of amphetamine psychosis, cited here for the symptom profile and for formication in about 40% of patients, rising to 70% among those with psychosis
Rylander's report of punding in 26% (40 of 150) of people with amphetamine addiction, the origin of the term

Klawans & Weiner: intravenous amphetamine worsened chorea in people with Sydenham, Huntington or lupus chorea but produced no movement disorder in controls, and the effect was prevented by a D2 antagonist
Volkow et al.: dopamine transporter reductions recovered significantly after more than 12 months of abstinence, cited here as an argument against a Parkinson's-like process
Moszczynska et al. 'Why is parkinsonism not a feature of human methamphetamine users?', the anatomical argument (caudate versus putamen; terminals versus cell bodies) adopted here
Johanson et al.: vesicular monoamine transporter binding not significantly reduced in people abstinent from methamphetamine, cited here as evidence for regulation rather than damage
Scott et al. meta-analysis of neurocognitive effects, cited here for the pattern of episodic memory, executive and motor deficits

Callaghan et al.: higher incidence of Parkinson's disease among hospital patients with methamphetamine-use disorders over 10 years; Christine et al. and Garwood et al.: earlier symptom onset and an odds ratio of 8 for amphetamine exposure in a telephone survey of patients versus spouses
First publication of this text in Neurologic Clinics 29(3)
Reprinted in Psychiatric Clinics of North America (this version)

replication.where_it_stands: A readable clinical synthesis whose value for this encyclopedia is as a pointer to the phenomena and to their primary literature, not as a source of numbers. The cognitive claims should rest on Scott et al. (2007) and the imaging ones on the primary PET and post-mortem studies already carded here; the Parkinson's question remains open and needs Callaghan et al. (2010) and the Garwood and Christine surveys read directly. Its figures for formication and punding come from amphetamine-era and cocaine samples and should not be cited as methamphetamine prevalences.

funding.funder: United States Public Health Service grants DA020484 and DA026867 (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: The author states he has nothing to disclose (Footnotes).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Emergency Medicine, Indiana University School of Medicine. Editorial assistance is acknowledged. The author's own research is on methamphetamine thermoregulation and toxicity, which is not the subject of this review.

what_would_settle_it: For frequency: a cohort of people who use methamphetamine recruited outside treatment settings, assessed with standardized instruments for psychotic symptoms, delusional infestation, repetitive behaviour and movement disorder, against a comparison group matched on other stimulant use and social circumstances. For the Parkinson's question: long-term follow-up of large cohorts with verified methamphetamine exposure into the age range of onset, with incidence and age at onset compared against unexposed people matched on smoking.

domains.note: A single-author commentary and review with no methods, search, dates or criteria, and no statement of how its sources were chosen.

Only one cited study is appraised: the Parkinson's telephone survey, called small and subject to recall bias. Elsewhere the figures are passed on as they stand, several from sources whose population or substance does not match the sentence they support (40% with abnormal testing from a study of people with HIV; the formication figures from a 1969 report and a 1967 description of amphetamine psychosis; the smoking proportions and the tobacco argument from one review), and one evaluation is asserted rather than shown (the meta-analysis is called well done, with no criteria).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Two self-citations in the reference list, both used as background for acute complications and hyperthermic syndromes; the substantive evidence is other groups' work.

Speculation runs through the text in the same voice as the evidence: the opening commentary states that methamphetamine slowly damages dopaminergic neurotransmission and preferentially causes psychiatric complications; the cognition section offers the metaphor of chemically converting a person into a modern Phineas Gage as an account of behaviour and decision-making; the choreoathetosis section suggests that many homeless people seen moving abnormally in city streets may be showing stimulant-induced choreoathetosis; and the Key Points state that dopamine receptor antagonists are the most effective treatment for the chronic psychiatric manifestations, with no trial cited anywhere in the article. The possibility that deficits precede use is raised twice in the body but in neither the commentary nor the summary.

domains.domain: Balance of drug-induced damage against pre-existing vulnerability and alternative explanations
domains.note: The Parkinson's section is genuinely balanced, setting the prevailing view that risk is not increased, with four supporting hypotheses, against the studies that suggest it is, and the psychosis section lays out the dual-diagnosis debate. Elsewhere the framing is categorical and causal, and the commentary, summary and key points carry only the damage reading.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review or commentary (METHODS §5.3), so the editors' narrative-review checklist is used; scoring it against AMSTAR 2 only restated that it is not a systematic review. The absence of any search or selection method fixes that domain at high, and the overall can be no milder than the worst domain, so the overall is high; appraisal of the cited studies and the separation of evidence from speculation are also high. The review is useful as a clinical description of phenomena a neurologist or psychiatrist may see, as a guide to the older amphetamine literature, and for the balanced Parkinson's section. Its percentages are second-hand and several are misattributed (see the reporting issues), so no figure should be cited from this paper, and nothing in it is evidence that a treatment works.

key_findings.finding: Cognition: about 40% of people who use methamphetamine are said to have abnormalities on neuropsychiatric tests; the pattern of deficits most often reported, per the cited meta-analysis, is episodic memory, executive function and motor function, with the largest impairments in episodic memory. Motor deficits are said to affect fine dexterity rather than gross movement, consistent with greater dopaminergic loss in the caudate than the putamen.
key_findings.note: The 40% figure is cited to Rippeth et al. (2004), which by title concerns neuropsychological impairment in people with HIV; the meta-analysis is Scott et al. (2007).

key_findings.finding: Psychosis: the symptom profile is described as similar to schizophrenia, most often persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations, sometimes with negative symptoms; both respond to dopamine antagonists. Psychosis is seen more readily with larger amounts used over longer periods; reported durations range from about a week to indefinite, and symptoms can return with renewed use or under stress.

The review sets out the dual-diagnosis alternative: people with a strong family history of mental illness are significantly more likely to develop methamphetamine-associated psychosis (Taiwanese studies), people with schizophrenia given small amounts of methamphetamine have symptom exacerbations, and methamphetamine may unmask psychosis in susceptible people, or be sought as self-treatment, or share a neuronal substrate with addiction risk.

Historical epidemiology as cited: an estimated 2 million people using methamphetamine in Japan in 1954 and as many as 200,000 with drug-induced psychosis between 1945 and 1955; a 2008 United Nations estimate of 25 million people using amphetamines worldwide, against 14 million for cocaine and 11 million for heroin.
key_findings.note: Both are second-hand. The 2023 World Drug Report figure cited by Hemphill et al. (2024) is 36 million for amphetamines.

key_findings.finding: Formication (delusional infestation, 'meth mites'): reported by about 40% of patients admitted to drug-treatment facilities and by about 70% of those who had ever had psychosis; repetitive skin picking can cause facial and limb scarring, and with poor hygiene raises the risk of skin infections including meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Dopamine antagonists with abstinence are said to help.
key_findings.note: The two sources cited for the 40% and 70% are from 1967 and 1969 and concern amphetamine and methylamphetamine, not clearly methamphetamine treatment admissions.

key_findings.finding: Punding (non-goal-directed repetitive activity): reported in 26% (40 of 150) of people with amphetamine addiction interviewed by Rylander in 1972, and in 38% of 50 people addicted to cocaine, who spent on average 3 hours a day on such activities, with one spending up to 14 hours. Behaviour often resembles the person's former occupation and differs by sex; most people described it without distress, and it usually abates with abstinence. Duration and amount of drug use did not predict who developed it, which the author reads as evidence of predisposition.
key_findings.note: The cocaine figures are attributed in the text to Fasano, but the 38% and the 3 hours carry reference 66, a 2010 review in Molecular Psychiatry, and the following sentences about the same patients carry reference 67, a 2009 review of dopamine dysregulation syndrome by a different group. The primary study is cited earlier in the same paragraph as reference 71 (Fasano and colleagues, 2008, on punding in cocaine addiction), so the figures are traceable, but not through the references attached to them.

key_findings.finding: Parkinson's disease: the author states the prevailing view is that methamphetamine use does not raise the risk, supported by four arguments: methamphetamine affects dopaminergic terminals rather than substantia nigra cell bodies; reductions are greater in the caudate than the putamen, the reverse of Parkinson's disease; transporter reductions recovered significantly after more than 12 months of abstinence; and vesicular monoamine transporter binding, which is reduced in Parkinson's disease and resistant to compensatory regulation, was not reduced in people abstinent from methamphetamine and was increased in one study of people not abstinent.
key_findings.locator: Chronic methamphetamine abuse and the development of Parkinson's disease, 2nd–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Against that view the review cites a 10-year hospital-records study reporting a higher incidence of Parkinson's disease among patients previously admitted with a methamphetamine-related problem, and two studies of the same group of patients: a telephone survey in which people with Parkinson's disease were significantly more likely than their unaffected spouses to have used amphetamines (odds ratio 8, interval 1.6 to 41.4, printed without a confidence level), with exposures about 27 years before symptom onset, and a second study in which those with a history of amphetamine use were significantly younger at symptom onset but not at diagnosis. The author notes that the survey is small and subject to recall bias.
key_findings.locator: Chronic methamphetamine abuse and the development of Parkinson's disease, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: The interval 1.6 to 41.4 is very wide and the comparison is between patients and their spouses, so the point estimate says little about magnitude. The review prints the interval without stating a confidence level, so any '95%' is the editors' assumption; editors' check: the geometric midpoint of 1.6 and 41.4 is 8.1, consistent with the printed odds ratio of 8. The earlier age at symptom onset comes from the second study, not from the telephone survey.

key_findings.finding: An alternative explanation offered for the absence of parkinsonism is tobacco: 87–92% of people who use methamphetamine smoke cigarettes against 22% of the general population, and smoking is inversely associated with Parkinson's disease, so this group may be partly protected.
key_findings.locator: Chronic methamphetamine abuse and the development of Parkinson's disease, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Both halves of this argument are second-hand from one review; the smoking proportions have no date, country or sample attached.

key_findings.finding: Choreoathetoid movements: reported in case reports with amphetamines and cocaine; in a 1974 experiment, intravenous amphetamine markedly worsened chorea in people with pre-existing chorea but produced no movement disorder in controls, and the effect was prevented by a D2 antagonist, which the investigators read as requiring prior striatal damage. Movements can persist for years after stopping, and can return on renewed use. Dopamine antagonists and benzodiazepines helped some patients and not others; the literature is sparse.

Dental disease ('meth mouth'): advanced caries, tooth loss and fractures are attributed to reduced saliva (via central alpha-2 adrenergic mechanisms), tooth grinding and jaw clenching by day and night, poor oral hygiene and frequent sugar-containing soft drinks; the caries pattern is said to resemble other dry-mouth conditions, affecting buccal surfaces of posterior teeth and interproximal areas of anterior teeth, and can progress to destruction of enamel with young patients needing dentures.
key_findings.note: No frequencies, denominators or comparison groups are given, and a specific soft-drink brand is named as the drink of choice.

key_findings.finding: Pharmacology as stated: methamphetamine enters monoamine neurons through the transporters and is taken into vesicles, where its high pKa disrupts the proton gradient so monoamines accumulate in the cytoplasm and are reverse-transported out; it also reduces reuptake and enzymatic breakdown. Its half-life is given as 12 hours against about 90 minutes for cocaine. Repeated use depletes dopamine stores and damages dopamine and serotonin terminals through oxidative stress, neuroinflammation and excitotoxicity, worsened by hyperthermia.
key_findings.note: Hemphill et al. (2024) give about 10 hours for methamphetamine and 0.5 to 1.5 hours for cocaine, citing Cruickshank & Dyer (2009), which is also this review's reference 16.

reporting_issues.issue: A footnote states that this article originally appeared in the August 2011 issue of Neurologic Clinics (volume 29, number 3), so the same text is published twice, under two DOIs and two years. The first reader also recorded that Kevil et al. (2019) cite the Neurologic Clinics version (2011;29:641-655) for the same content; that is outside this source and has not been re-checked.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reference record must not count the two versions as independent sources, and claims citing 'Rusyniak 2011' and 'Rusyniak 2013' are citing one text.

reporting_issues.issue: The figure that about 40% of people who use methamphetamine have abnormalities on neuropsychiatric tests is cited to Rippeth et al. (2004), whose title is about neuropsychological impairment in people with HIV infection.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not usable as a general prevalence of cognitive impairment; the primary study's sample was selected on HIV status.

reporting_issues.issue: The formication figures (about 40%, rising to 70% in those who had experienced psychosis), described as coming from studies of patients admitted to drug-treatment facilities for methamphetamine use, are cited to a 1969 British report on methylamphetamine (both figures) and to a 1967 description of amphetamine psychosis (the 70% carries that source alone). Neither is a study of admissions to a methamphetamine treatment facility. The substance mismatch applies only to the 1967 source: methylamphetamine in the 1969 title is an older name for methamphetamine, not a different drug.
reporting_issues.consequence: The setting does not match the description for either figure, and the substance does not match for the 1967 source, so these cannot be cited as prevalences among people admitted for methamphetamine treatment; both primary papers must be read first.

reporting_issues.issue: The punding figures for cocaine (38% of 50 patients, average 3 hours a day) are attributed in the text to Fasano but cited to reference 66, a 2010 Molecular Psychiatry review by Fasano and Petrovic, and the following sentences about the same patients are cited to reference 67, a 2009 review of dopamine dysregulation syndrome by a different group. The underlying primary study is cited earlier in the same paragraph, as reference 71 (Fasano and colleagues, 2008, on punding in cocaine addiction), but not at the sentences that carry its figures.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures are traceable, but through reference 71 rather than the references attached to them; they should be taken from that 2008 primary study and not cited through this review.

reporting_issues.issue: Scheduling is attributed to the wrong agency: the text says the Food and Drug Administration has characterized methamphetamine as a schedule II drug (scheduling under the Controlled Substances Act is administered by the Drug Enforcement Administration). The Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act is dated 2005 here and 2006 by Hemphill et al. (2024).
reporting_issues.consequence: Regulatory statements should not be taken from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The Key Points state that dopamine receptor antagonists are the most effective treatments for the chronic psychiatric manifestations of methamphetamine use; the body cites no comparative trial, only a 1974 study of a neuroleptic against amphetamine-induced symptoms, a 1992 hypothesis paper on formication and a suggestion in a review that atypical antipsychotics might be tried for punding.
reporting_issues.consequence: A treatment claim without supporting trials; the encyclopedia's treatment claims must come from trials or systematic reviews.

reporting_issues.issue: The review is addressed inconsistently to its readership: the opening commentary and Key Points speak to psychiatrists and psychologists, while the introduction and body say the article should help the practising neurologist, a trace of its first publication in a neurology journal.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cosmetic, but it confirms the reprint status and means the framing was not revised for the new audience.

reporting_issues.issue: Almost no number in the review carries a denominator, interval or comparison group. The exceptions are the Rylander punding count (40 of 150), the cocaine punding figure (38% of 50 patients) and the Parkinson's odds ratio with its interval; the smoking proportions (87-92% against 22%) have no sample, country or date attached.
reporting_issues.consequence: Nothing in this review can anchor a quantitative claim; each figure must be taken from its primary source.

reporting_issues.issue: Read from the NIH author manuscript. The page shows the print citation (Psychiatr Clin North Am 2013;36(2):261-275, final edited form dated 11 April 2013) but no page numbers within the text. The header line above it reads that the author manuscript became available in PMC on 1 June 2014, which is a PMC availability date and not an issue date.
reporting_issues.consequence: Anchors are to section headings of the author manuscript rather than printed pages. The citation year is 2013; there is no June 2013 date in this source, and the earlier reading of one was a misreading of the PMC availability line.

reporting_issues.issue: The review states at the end of the pharmacology and toxicology section that the similarities in pharmacology, toxicology and clinical effects between methamphetamine, amphetamine and other stimulants such as cocaine and MDMA make the discussion of neurologic complications that follows largely translatable to those drugs. No evidence is offered for that translation, and several of the review's own figures are in fact about amphetamine or cocaine.
reporting_issues.consequence: This encyclopedia files claims per substance. Nothing in this review may be moved between substances on the strength of that sentence, and each figure must be checked for which drug it concerns before it is used.

reporting_issues.issue: Two speculative passages are presented in the same voice as the evidence. In the cognition paragraphs the review writes that people whose episodic memory is damaged may be doomed to repeat past mistakes and that methamphetamine chemically converts a person into a modern Phineas Gage. In the choreoathetosis section it suggests that many homeless people seen dancing and writhing on city street corners may be manifesting stimulant-induced choreoathetoid movements, offering as support only the existence of street names for the phenomenon.
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither passage is evidence, and the second is an unevidenced inference about a vulnerable group; under METHODS §9 neither may be carried into any monograph, in paraphrase or otherwise.

reporting_issues.issue: Three statements in the history and epidemiology section rest on sources that cannot be cited. The fall in methamphetamine treatment admissions in 2006, the first in ten years, is attributed to the 2005 precursor legislation on the authority of one secondary review. The cost of production and the earnings of a small producer (about 200 dollars against 2000 to 5000 dollars) are cited to a university web page with a January 2011 access date. The worldwide figures of 25 million people using amphetamines against 14 million for cocaine and 11 million for heroin are cited to a United Nations annual report, also as a web address with a 2011 access date.
reporting_issues.consequence: A policy-effect claim from a single secondary source and figures from web pages that may no longer resolve. None of the three may be cited from this review; the policy claim needs a primary analysis and the prevalence figures the current World Drug Report, under the epidemiology rules (METHODS §10).

reporting_issues.issue: The review's vocabulary throughout is that of the older literature: it calls use abuse, labels people by their drug use, and frames the subject as an epidemic, including in the summary, which speaks of devastating effects.
reporting_issues.consequence: Every paraphrase from this source must be reworded in person-first language (METHODS §9), as this card does, and the review's adjectives of alarm must not travel with its content.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3764482 (NIH author manuscript; all sections, the Key Points box, acknowledgments, funding, footnotes, author affiliation and the full 113-entry reference list; the article has no tables or figures; no supplementary material)

disagreements.reviewer: content confirmed; the span should be ¶1-3, not ¶1-4: the 40% figure, the cited meta-analysis and episodic memory are in ¶1, executive function in ¶2, fine-motor dexterity and the caudate-versus-putamen argument in ¶3; ¶4 is the anxiety, depression and psychosis paragraph
disagreements.resolution: Corrected to the 1st to 3rd paragraphs. Recounted in the source: the section has seven paragraphs of running text, and the three this finding covers are the first three. The note is also confirmed: the 40% is cited to reference 26, which the reference list gives as a study of neuropsychological impairment in people with HIV, and the meta-analysis is reference 27.

disagreements.reviewer: content confirmed; the right span is ¶6-7, and the section has seven paragraphs, so there is no ¶8: the symptom profile and the response to dopamine antagonists are in ¶6, the amount-and-duration, variability and recurrence statements in ¶7
disagreements.resolution: Corrected to the 6th and 7th paragraphs, after recounting the section (¶1 cognition, ¶2 executive function, ¶3 motor, ¶4 mental illnesses, ¶5 post-war Japan, ¶6 symptom profile and treatment response, ¶7 dose, duration and the dual-diagnosis debate).

disagreements.reviewer: content confirmed; it is ¶7, not ¶8: all four strands (family history, exacerbation in people with schizophrenia, unmasking, self-treatment and a shared neuronal substrate) are in that one long paragraph
disagreements.resolution: Corrected to the 7th paragraph, the last of the section, which carries all four strands in sequence.

disagreements.first_pass: The cocaine figures are attributed to Fasano, but the reference given is a 2010 review in Molecular Psychiatry and the following sentences are cited to a separate 2009 review; the primary study is not identified.
disagreements.reviewer: content confirmed, but the note is wrong on one point: the primary cocaine study is cited in the same paragraph as reference 71, where the review introduces punding in people who used cocaine; what is wrong is the citation at sentence level
disagreements.resolution: Accepted and the note rewritten. Checked in the source: the punding paragraph cites reference 71 when it introduces punding in people who used cocaine, and the reference list gives 71 as a 2008 primary study of punding in cocaine addiction, while the 38% and the 3 hours carry reference 66 (a 2010 review) and the sentences that follow carry reference 67 (a 2009 review by another group). So the figures can be traced, through the right reference rather than the ones attached. Reporting issue 3 is corrected to match.

disagreements.first_pass: Chronic methamphetamine abuse and the development of Parkinson's disease, 2nd–4th paragraphs
disagreements.reviewer: content confirmed; the span should be Parkinson's ¶2-3, not ¶2-4: the first three arguments are in ¶2 and the vesicular-transporter argument in ¶3, while ¶4 is the tobacco argument
disagreements.resolution: Corrected to the 2nd and 3rd paragraphs. The section has five paragraphs of running text: ¶1 impulse-control parallels and the striatal findings, ¶2 the prevailing view with the terminals-versus-cell-bodies, caudate-versus-putamen and recovery-after-12-months arguments, ¶3 the vesicular transporter argument, ¶4 nicotine, ¶5 the contrary evidence.

disagreements.first_pass: locator: Chronic methamphetamine abuse and the development of Parkinson's disease, 6th paragraph | finding attributed the age-at-onset result to the telephone survey and printed the interval as 95% CI
disagreements.reviewer: content is in Parkinson's ¶5, not ¶6 (the section has five paragraphs); the review presents two studies of the same group of patients and the earlier age at symptom onset comes from the second, not the survey; and the interval is printed without a level, so '95% CI' is the card's addition
disagreements.resolution: All three accepted. Locator corrected to the 5th paragraph; the finding now says that two studies share one patient group and attributes the age-at-onset result to the second of them, which the reference list identifies as a 2010 paper on parkinsonism in people with a history of amphetamine exposure, the survey being a 2006 paper; and the interval is now given without a confidence level, with the assumption flagged in the note. I recomputed the geometric midpoint of the interval as 8.1, consistent with the printed odds ratio.

disagreements.first_pass: Chronic methamphetamine abuse and the development of Parkinson's disease, 5th paragraph
disagreements.reviewer: content confirmed (87-92% against 22%, and smoking inversely associated with Parkinson's disease, so possible partial protection); the location is ¶4, not ¶5
disagreements.resolution: Corrected to the 4th paragraph. The note is confirmed as well: both halves are second-hand from reference 84, a 2009 review of the impact of cigarette smoking on stimulant addiction, and the smoking proportions carry no sample, country or date.

disagreements.first_pass: A footnote states that this article originally appeared in the August 2011 issue of Neurologic Clinics (29(3)); the text is therefore published twice under two DOIs and two years. Kevil et al. (2019) cite the Neurologic Clinics version (2011;29:641–655) for the same content.
disagreements.reviewer: partly-confirmed: the footnote is confirmed, and the consequence is right and important; the statement about how Kevil et al. (2019) cite it, including the page range, is outside this source and was not checked
disagreements.resolution: Reworded. The footnote is confirmed verbatim in the Footnotes block of the saved page. The cross-reference to Kevil et al. is now marked as single-reader and unchecked; the consequence, that the two versions are one text and must not be counted as independent sources, stands.

disagreements.first_pass: The formication figures (about 40%, rising to 70% in those with psychosis), described as coming from studies of patients admitted to drug-treatment facilities for methamphetamine use, are cited to Hawks et al. (1969, a British report on methylamphetamine) and Ellinwood (1967, a description of amphetamine psychosis).
disagreements.reviewer: corrected: the citations and the mismatch of setting are confirmed, but 'methylamphetamine' in the 1969 title is an older name for methamphetamine, not a different substance, so the substance objection applies to the 1967 amphetamine source only
disagreements.resolution: Accepted and reworded. The issue now separates the setting objection, which applies to both, from the substance objection, which applies to the 1967 source.
